name: Dynamic Light Variation as Sustained Temporal PE Engagement
mechanism_chain_provenance: INHERITED from Document 34 (L5) — structural pattern preserved; quantitative parameters newly established in LIGHT-I

mechanism_chain.description: Architectural light source with temporal variation in luminance, CCT, or spectral composition

data.finding: Natural daylight provides continuous luminance variation from cloud passage, solar angle change, and weather dynamics; variation frequencies 0.01-2.0 cycles/min
data.effect: Continuous low-to-moderate amplitude variation in daylit spaces

justification.backing: Dynamic variation is inherent in daylight through windows. Cloud passage, solar angle change, and seasonal variation all produce temporal dynamics. Artificial lighting is typically static unless programmed with dynamic control.
justification.qualifier: The dynamic profile of daylight depends on climate, weather, and building orientation. Overcast conditions reduce variation amplitude; clear sky with intermittent clouds maximizes it.
justification.rebuttal: This step would fail if: (a) building users prefer static lighting and deploy shading to eliminate variation; (b) dynamic variation from daylight is below perceptual threshold in typical conditions.

mechanism_chain.description: → PP channel: visual cortex generates predictions about luminance level at next timestep based on prior trajectory

data.finding: Visual cortex generates temporal predictions about stimulus trajectory; prediction errors drive attention and adaptation
data.effect: Temporal prediction is intrinsic to hierarchical predictive processing

justification.backing: The predictive processing framework posits that all perceptual systems generate predictions at multiple timescales. Luminance prediction follows naturally from this framework.
justification.qualifier: The specific mechanism by which luminance variation produces PE engagement is theoretical. The PP framework is general; direct measurement of luminance PE in architectural settings is absent.
justification.rebuttal: This step would fail if: (a) luminance adaptation fully absorbs variation before prediction mechanisms engage; (b) the PP framework does not accurately describe visual cortex operation.

mechanism_chain.description: → If variation rate within engagement zone: moderate continuous luminance PE → sustained mild orienting response → prevents visual habituation to static scene

data.finding: Dynamic light produces approximately 18% larger alertness and engagement effects than equivalent static light at same mean level
data.source: Veitch & Newsham (1998); Viola et al. (2008) indirect comparison

justification.backing: The available evidence suggests a modest bonus for dynamic variation over static lighting. Panel consensus was that dynamic variation is 'sufficient but not strictly necessary' for engagement benefits.
justification.qualifier: This is flagged as THEORETICAL_DEFAULT. Direct comparison of dynamic vs. static at matched mean levels in occupied building settings is sparse. The 18% bonus is derived from cross-study comparison, not controlled experimentation.
justification.rebuttal: This step would fail if: (a) the apparent dynamic bonus is confounded with other differences between daylit and artificially lit spaces; (b) habituation to dynamic variation eliminates the engagement benefit over days/weeks; (c) Laike's field data showing effects from sustained bright light without emphasis on variation are more representative.

competing_accounts.claim: Field data do not show that dynamic variation is necessary for circadian health outcomes — sustained bright light without particular emphasis on variation may be adequate
competing_accounts.implication_for_template: If sustained irradiance is sufficient, the dynamic variation template (L5) adds only marginal value above L2/L3; the engagement benefit is real but small

mechanism_chain.description: → CB channel (dawn/dusk transitions): rate-of-change in melanopic irradiance provides temporal derivative signal to SCN (in addition to integral irradiance) → sharpens circadian phase anchoring

data.finding: Dawn and dusk transitions are the most potent circadian phase-shifting periods; a building providing gradual 30-60 minute ramps produces more efficient entrainment than abrupt transitions
data.effect: Improved circadian phase anchoring with gradual transitions

data.finding: Animal studies using skeleton photoperiods suggest temporal structure of light, not just integral, matters for entrainment quality

justification.backing: Foster's argument that the temporal derivative of melanopic irradiance is itself a circadian signal suggests that dawn/dusk ramps provide value beyond simple on/off transitions. Architectural lighting controls that program gradual transitions may improve entrainment quality.
justification.qualifier: The magnitude of the temporal derivative benefit in occupied buildings is not quantified. The ≥15 m-lux per 30 minutes ramp rate is the panel's consensus estimate for the minimum effective dawn/dusk transition.
justification.rebuttal: This step would fail if: (a) the temporal derivative signal is negligible relative to the irradiance integral; (b) real building dawn/dusk transitions (affected by shading, orientation, weather) do not provide clean gradients; (c) behavioral patterns (arrival/departure times) override architectural dawn/dusk programming.

mechanism_chain.description: → If variation too slow (< 0.01 cycles/min sustained): full adaptation, no PE engagement, equivalent to static light for cognitive purposes

data.finding: Luminance adaptation operates on timescales of seconds to minutes; variation slower than adaptation rate does not produce sustained PE
data.source: Panel consensus; derived from adaptation literature
data.effect: Adaptation eliminates PE for slow variation

justification.backing: The visual system adapts to ambient luminance level. If variation is slower than the adaptation timescale, the system tracks the level without generating prediction errors.
justification.qualifier: The 0.01 cycles/min threshold is an estimate based on adaptation dynamics, not directly measured in architectural settings.
justification.rebuttal: This step would fail if: (a) the adaptation timescale is much longer than assumed, such that slow variation still generates PE; (b) cognitive effects of light variation operate through a different mechanism than luminance PE.

mechanism_chain.description: → If variation too fast (> 2.0 cycles/min at high amplitude): distraction, discomfort, or flicker response — aversive range

data.finding: High-frequency flicker (>3 Hz) produces visual discomfort, headaches, and in susceptible individuals, photosensitive seizures; temporal frequency and amplitude interact to determine discomfort threshold
data.effect: Discomfort and adverse responses above threshold

justification.backing: High-frequency variation is aversive. IEEE standards specify acceptable flicker limits for lighting. The 2.0 cycles/min upper bound for beneficial variation is well below the problematic flicker range.
justification.qualifier: The aversive threshold depends on amplitude as well as frequency. Low-amplitude high-frequency variation may be imperceptible; high-amplitude low-frequency variation may be engaging rather than aversive. The 2.0 cycles/min at high amplitude is the panel's boundary estimate.
justification.rebuttal: This step would fail if: (a) individuals differ substantially in flicker sensitivity such that some find 2+ cycles/min engaging while others find it aversive; (b) habituation reduces discomfort over exposure time.

prediction_error_signal.note: Minimum amplitude of luminance variation (as fraction of mean) required to maintain sustained PE engagement. Below 8%: below JND threshold for most observers; above 35% at high frequency: discomfort range.
prediction_error_signal.source: Derived from contrast sensitivity function literature; Blackwell (1946) threshold data

temporal_rhythm.note: Rate of change in melanopic irradiance during simulated dawn/dusk that produces a measurable improvement in circadian phase anchoring relative to abrupt transitions. Foster's analysis of PRC sensitivity to rate-of-change vs. magnitude.
temporal_rhythm.source: Foster (theoretical); Gooley et al. (2010) dawn simulation study

effect_size.note: Dynamic light produces approximately 18% larger alertness and engagement effects than equivalent static light at the same mean level. This is the bonus coefficient for dynamic variation above the static baseline. Small effect size but consistently positive across available studies.
effect_size.source: Veitch & Newsham (1998); Viola et al. (2008) indirect comparison
effect_size.flag: THEORETICAL_DEFAULT — direct comparison of dynamic vs. static at matched mean levels in occupied building settings is sparse

### Template VIEW1: Nature View as Multi-Channel Prediction Confirmation

template_id: "NATURE_VIEW_CONVERGENCE_001"
display_id: "VIEW1"
name: "Nature View as Multi-Channel Prediction Confirmation — How Visual Access to Natural Environments Produces Convergent Stress Reduction, Attention Restoration, and Positive Affect"

structural_pattern: >
  A window view of nature engages multiple PE mechanisms
  simultaneously, producing a convergent effect that exceeds
  the sum of individual channels. This structural parallel to
  L3 (daylight convergence) and MAT4 (wood convergence) is the
  template's central insight: nature views are powerful not
  because of any single mechanism but because they confirm
  predictions across MANY channels at once.
  
  FIVE CONVERGENT CHANNELS:
  
  CHANNEL 1 — FRACTAL FLUENCY (T1): Natural scenes exhibit
  1/f spatial frequency profiles with fractal dimension near
  D ≈ 1.3 (Taylor et al., 2011). This matches the visual
  system's processing structure, producing maximal processing
  fluency and minimal visual PE. Trees, clouds, water surfaces,
  and terrain all exhibit fractal statistics. Built environments
  typically exhibit non-fractal statistics (regular geometry,
  flat surfaces, periodic repetition). The nature view confirms
  the visual system's deep prediction for natural spatial
  statistics.
  
  CHANNEL 2 — PROSPECT AND SPATIAL DEPTH (SC2/T5): Nature
  views typically provide spatial depth (long isovist) with
  vegetative partial enclosure — the prospect-refuge combination
  that Appleton (1975) identified and SC2 formalizes. The
  ability to see far (prospect) with the protection of an
  enclosed space (refuge through the building itself) confirms
  the spatial prediction for safety: the occupant can monitor
  the environment for threats and opportunities while being
  protected. A view of a brick wall provides neither prospect
  nor spatial depth.
  
  CHANNEL 3 — ATTENTION RESTORATION (T25/ART): Natural scenes
  engage "soft fascination" — involuntary attention to gently
  interesting stimuli (moving leaves, drifting clouds, flowing
  water) that permits directed attention to rest and recover
  (Kaplan, 1995). This is the attentional Goldilocks zone:
  enough engagement to prevent disengagement, insufficient
  demand to deplete directed attention. A blank wall provides
  no fascination; a busy urban scene provides hard fascination
  that demands effortful processing.
  
  CHANNEL 4 — TEMPORAL VARIATION (L5): Nature views are
  inherently dynamic: wind moves branches, clouds shift,
  light changes, seasons transform the scene. This dynamic
  variation provides the temporal PE that L5 formalizes —
  gradual, natural change that maintains interest without
  producing surprise. The view of nature is a built-in
  dynamic light and pattern display that changes continuously
  through the day and across seasons.
  
  CHANNEL 5 — ECOLOGICAL SAFETY SIGNAL: Green vegetation,
  water, and spatial openness are evolutionary signals of
  a resource-rich, safe environment (Ulrich et al., 1991).
  This is the biophilia/SRT mechanism: the presence of
  nature signals environmental safety, reducing HPA axis
  activation (T5) and contributing to allostatic balance
  (T29). Built environments lack this signal; degraded
  environments (dead vegetation, polluted water) may
  invert it.
  
  CONVERGENCE: Each channel contributes a modest individual
  effect. The convergent total — all five channels confirming
  predictions simultaneously — produces a strong, multi-
  mechanism benefit that explains why nature views consistently
  produce measurable health outcomes (Ulrich, 1984; White
  et al., 2019) while individual mechanisms produce smaller
  effects in isolation. The structural parallel to L3 and
  MAT4 is deliberate: MULTI-CHANNEL CONVERGENCE IS A GENERAL
  PRINCIPLE of how natural stimuli produce strong effects.

cross_template_interactions.IC2: Modest interaction: dynamic variation reduces perceptual monotony costs at the body-budget level; the absence of variation in deep-plan spaces under fixed artificial lighting constitutes a mild persistent sensory-prediction flatness that IC2 registers as a low-grade environmental impoverishment signal
cross_template_interactions.AX4: High AX4 interaction: occupants with operable shading, skylights, or window access naturally receive dynamic variation from weather and solar angle; those without control have static artificial light as their only option. Perceived control over light dynamics is a significant moderator of the effect.
